title: Quantifying cell shape and density fluctuations in epithelial tissue in vivo
authors: Jake Turley, Helen Weavers, Paul Martin, Isaac V. Chenchiah, Tanniemola B. Liverpool
abstract: Controlling changes in cell shape are crucial for many biological processes, such as tissue development and wound healing. Tissues typically are heterogeneous with a variety of cell shapes and sizes. Of particular interest are local deviations from an average cell shape and size. These fluctuations may extend and transmit across tissues, potentially offering valuable insights into tissue characteristics such as variations in effective "stiffness" or rigidity. In this study, we present a theoretical framework that captures the dynamics of epithelial cell shapes within tissue, incorporating both their average behaviour and fluctuation patterns. We model cells as interacting soft ellipsoids of varying size and aspect ratio. Coarse-graining our model, we obtain a set of continuum stochastic differential equations from which we derive spatial-temporal correlation functions. These correlation functions fit with our experimental data from the developmental process of the \textit{Drosophila} pupal wing. From the correlation functions, critical parameters representing active cell shape changes and effective tissue "stiffness" can be determined.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework to model cell shape and density fluctuations in living epithelial tissues, using the developing Drosophila wing as an experimental system. By coarse-graining a microscopic model, the authors derive continuum stochastic equations whose parameters allow them to quantify active remodeling forces and passive tissue stiffness. The results demonstrate that these parameters can be extracted by fitting the model to measured spatial and temporal correlation functions.
main_problem: The study quantifies cell shape and density fluctuations in epithelial tissue in vivo to gain insights into the tissue's mechanical properties, such as effective stiffness.
main_result: The theoretical framework successfully models the dynamics by separating active shape remodeling contributions from passive mechanical stiffness, showing that active remodeling is crucial for processes like wound healing.
method: The authors developed a theoretical framework involving continuum stochastic differential equations derived from a microscopic model of interacting soft ellipsoids, which are then fitted to experimental correlation functions.
model_or_system: The system is epithelial tissue, studied using time-lapse imaging of the developing Drosophila pupal wing. Cells are modeled as interacting soft ellipsoids, and the dynamics are coarse-grained into continuum fields for density and shape fluctuations.
key_observables: Density correlation function (C_rho_rho), Q-tensor correlation function (C_alpha_alpha^qq), mean density (rho), and mean elongation (Q(1)).
important_parameters: Active shape remodeling parameter (A), effective tissue stiffness (L), and diffusion coefficients (D_r, D_q).
main_assumptions: The model relies on coarse-graining approximations, linearization around mean fields, and assuming the P/D axis aligns with global tension.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate cell shape fluctuations in the pupal wing, the soft ellipsoid model, the linear increase of mean density and elongation over time, and correlation functions showing decay rates near wounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical problem and microscopic model to deriving continuum stochastic equations for fluctuations, calculating correlation functions in k-space, and finally applying the model to fit and interpret experimental data from wounding and genetic perturbations.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of continuum stochastic field theories to biological soft matter systems provides a powerful analogy for modeling complex, fluctuating many-body systems, which shares mathematical structure with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics problems.
